claims.text: An optimized tungsten interlayer will enable a tunable transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
Tungsten has low intrinsic diffusivity at lower homologous temperatures.
Tungsten can accommodate dislocation activity at elevated stresses or temperatures.
The initial HEA multilayers lack an interlayer designed to mediate between diffusion-controlled and dislocation-controlled creep.
Adding a tungsten interlayer can create coherent or near-coherent interfaces in the HEA multilayer.
Lower homologous temperatures and stresses favor diffusion-mediated creep, whereas higher temperatures or stresses promote dislocation-mediated deformation.
The tungsten interlayer functions as a transitional interfacial phase between the HEA layers.
Tungsten's low diffusivity suppresses diffusion-mediated creep at lower temperatures.
At higher temperature or stress, tungsten's mechanical properties facilitate activation of dislocation motion.
The proposed dual behavior of tungsten bridges diffusion-controlled and dislocation-controlled creep regimes.
The tungsten interlayer will reduce creep strain rates at lower temperatures by suppressing diffusion.
Increasing temperature or stress will produce a transition to dislocation-dominated creep.
The tungsten interlayer will enhance overall creep resistance.
HEA multilayers without tungsten have a less controlled or singular creep mechanism because their interface coherency is uncontrolled.
The creep response is sensitive to tungsten-layer thickness.
The creep response is sensitive to the degree of interface coherency.
Severe irradiation may adversely affect tungsten-interlayer performance.
Severe oxidation may affect tungsten-interlayer performance.
